paragraphs: The paper organizes ethical alignment around a separation of responsibilities inspired by government. A language model generates knowledge, a component called DIKE establishes ethical guardrails, and ERIS interprets those guardrails in context. These components interact while remaining independent, making generation, rule setting, and contextual judgment distinct parts of the system.

The framework also introduces emotional conditioning as a way to influence linguistic behavior. Drawing on psychological accounts of how regulating emotion can prevent harmful behavior, the authors build a self-supervised pipeline that learns connections between emotions and language. These learned connections provide a mechanism for adjusting how the model expresses itself.

The authors combine this behavioral modulation with adversarial testing to demonstrate how DIKE and ERIS can guide language toward ethical outcomes. The contribution joins an organizational design with a learned behavioral mechanism: separate oversight components establish and interpret constraints, while emotional conditioning helps shape responses. The stated demonstration concerns this coordinated framework and its preservation of independent responsibilities, rather than a universal guarantee of ethical behavior.
icml-2025-a-checks-and-balances-framewor.tldr: A three-component alignment framework combines independent ethical oversight, contextual interpretation, and emotional conditioning to guide language-model behavior.

paragraphs: Multimodal models can receive several kinds of input yet learn to depend on only some of them. This paper examines how that collapse can arise inside the component that combines modalities. Its explanation centers on noisy features from one modality sharing neurons with useful features from another, obscuring the useful information in the first modality.

The authors also analyze why cross-modal knowledge distillation can help. They prove that it implicitly separates these tangled representations by relieving rank bottlenecks in the student encoder. In their analysis, this reduces noise in the fusion outputs without harming predictive features from either modality. The issue is therefore tied to how representational capacity is allocated across inputs.

Building on that account, the paper proposes explicitly reallocating representation bases to prevent collapse. The method also has applications when some modalities are missing. Experiments across multiple multimodal benchmarks support the theoretical claims. Together, the analysis and algorithm connect a model's apparent neglect of an input to a concrete interaction between noise, shared neurons, and restricted representation capacity.
icml-2025-a-closer-look-at-multimodal-re.tldr: The paper explains modality collapse through entangled noisy and predictive features and proposes reallocating representation capacity to prevent it.

paragraphs: As graph neural networks become deeper, their representations of different nodes can become increasingly alike. This oversmoothing weakens their ability to express distinctions within a graph. The paper interprets this behavior through dynamical systems: repeated network updates converge toward low-dimensional attractor states, producing the loss of representational diversity.

That interpretation motivates DYNAMO-GAT, a graph attention method that dynamically prunes attention weights. It combines noise-driven covariance analysis with Anti-Hebbian learning to guide this pruning. The intended effect is to preserve distinct attractor states, connecting a change in the network's attention structure to the behavior of its repeated updates.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees for the method and report stronger performance than existing approaches on benchmark datasets while using fewer computational resources. These findings make the dynamical-systems perspective relevant both as an explanation and as a design tool. The contribution is a pruning strategy grounded in an account of why deeper graph networks lose distinctions, with theoretical and experimental support for retaining those distinctions.
icml-2025-a-dynamical-systems-inspired-p.tldr: DYNAMO-GAT uses a dynamical-systems account of oversmoothing to prune attention weights and preserve distinct node representations.

paragraphs: Human preferences involve several criteria, but people do not always try to maximize all of them simultaneously. The paper draws on satisficing: prioritize one objective while keeping other considerations above acceptable thresholds. SITAlign turns this decision-making idea into a framework for aligning language-model outputs during inference.

The framework maximizes a primary objective subject to threshold constraints on secondary criteria. For example, helpfulness can be the quantity to improve while harmlessness must meet a specified standard. This formulation gives the secondary criteria a concrete role in defining acceptable responses. The authors also derive sub-optimality bounds to characterize how the approach compares with an optimum.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks support SITAlign's effectiveness. On PKU-SafeRLHF, the authors report a 22.3% margin over a leading multi-objective decoding strategy in GPT-4 win-tie rate for helpfulness reward, while meeting the harmlessness threshold. This result supports the approach in the evaluated setting: explicitly prioritizing helpfulness within a constrained acceptable set can improve the measured outcome while respecting the selected secondary requirement.
icml-2025-bounded-rationality-for-llms-s.tldr: SITAlign guides inference by maximizing a primary preference while requiring secondary criteria to satisfy acceptable thresholds.

paragraphs: Decision trees offer interpretable predictions, but finding an optimal sparse tree is a difficult optimization problem. Many practical methods use depth-first search, which becomes inefficient at greater depths and requires a maximum-depth setting. Best-first search offers another route, but its larger memory demands make careful use of the problem's structure important.

The paper formulates tree learning as an AND/OR graph search and introduces Branches, an algorithm based on AO*. This representation organizes alternative choices and the subproblems that must be solved together. It gives the search algorithm a structure tailored to decision-tree optimization, addressing the efficiency concerns that accompany a best-first approach.

The authors prove optimality and complexity guarantees and report efficiency improvements over the state of the art in both analysis and experiments. Branches also supports non-binary features, a capability they show can produce further computational gains. The contribution combines an exact optimization method with a broader feature representation, showing that both search organization and support for non-binary inputs can matter for efficient tree learning.
icml-2025-branches-efficiently-seeking-o.tldr: Branches uses AO*-style AND/OR graph search to find optimal sparse decision trees efficiently, including trees with non-binary features.

paragraphs: Federated multi-view clustering groups data whose different views are distributed across devices. Existing approaches often introduce global information only through pseudo-labels used later in clustering. This paper addresses the missed opportunity to use global structure during feature extraction, alongside the less-explored challenge of missing data in this setting.

FIMCFG gives each client a graph convolutional encoder with two heads. One extracts features containing global information, while the other captures information specific to a view. A fused graph then guides the combination of these representations into higher-level features, which support clustering under pseudo-label supervision. Global structure thus influences how the representations themselves are formed.

Clients upload those higher-level features to the server, where they refine graph fusion and pseudo-label computation. This creates a feedback process between local representations and shared guidance. The authors report extensive experiments demonstrating the method's effectiveness and superiority. Its central contribution is to connect global graph information with both feature learning and clustering in a federated setting that includes incomplete views.
icml-2025-federated-incomplete-multi-vie.tldr: FIMCFG uses a globally fused graph to guide local feature extraction and clustering when distributed multi-view data are incomplete.

paragraphs: Grouped datasets can contain both shared measurements and variables that exist only for particular groups. In cancer studies, for example, molecular measurements may be shared while some clinical information is specific to a cancer type. Clustering methods that use only common variables leave this additional information out of the grouping process.

The paper introduces the global-local, or GLocal, Dirichlet process to incorporate both kinds of variables. This Bayesian nonparametric model represents shared structure across groups alongside their local characteristics. The authors characterize it through a stick-breaking representation and as the limit of a finite mixture model, providing two mathematical descriptions of the same construction.

The analysis also quantifies approximation errors for a truncated prior, a corresponding finite mixture, and the resulting posterior. These results connect the model's mathematical definition to finite approximations used in computation. A fast variational Bayes algorithm supports scalable inference, illustrated through simulations and a TCGA pan-gastrointestinal cancer dataset. The contribution makes group-specific measurements part of clustering while analyzing the approximations needed to fit the model.
icml-2025-global-local-dirichlet-process.tldr: GLocal Dirichlet processes cluster grouped data using both shared and group-specific variables, with analyzed approximations and scalable inference.

paragraphs: Analog circuit topology design requires substantial manual work to meet application-specific requirements. Language models can generate circuit structures from specifications, but the prior formulation discussed here has two weaknesses: its token count grows quadratically with the number of vertices, and it responds inadequately to precise numerical inputs.

LaMAGIC2 introduces a succinct float-input canonical formulation with identifiers, called SFCI. Identifiers improve recognition of component types, while the new representation reduces token-length growth from quadratic to linear in the number of vertices. It also improves sensitivity to numerical precision, targeting situations where a generated circuit must meet tightly specified requirements.

Experiments report 34% higher success rates at a tolerance of 0.01 and mean squared errors ten times lower than a prior method. Transfer to circuits with more vertices also improves, by up to 58.5%. These results connect representation design with both efficiency and specification matching: a shorter encoding can also communicate component identity and numerical requirements more effectively in the evaluated circuit-generation tasks.
icml-2025-lamagic2-advanced-circuit-form.tldr: LaMAGIC2 improves circuit-generation accuracy and transferability with a linear-length representation that better conveys component identities and numerical specifications.

paragraphs: This paper adds a diffusion-based way for pretrained language models to spend more computation when answering a problem. The authors report that increasing diffusion steps produces monotonically improving accuracy in their evaluations. This connects additional inference work directly to better downstream performance for the models they fine-tune.

The method also supports guidance techniques for answering questions on particular topics. Adaptive ordinary differential equation solvers let the model determine the computation needed for a problem, giving the framework a way to vary effort across inputs. These capabilities extend the role of diffusion beyond simply using a fixed number of refinement steps.

The authors state that the method applies to foundation models pretrained with cross-entropy and leaves their original weights unchanged, preserving single-step generation capabilities. It is also compatible with conventional fine-tuning and search, and can be more effective than those approaches. Its significance is an additional route to scaling inference computation that can coexist with existing adaptation methods while connecting autoregressive models to diffusion-based generation.
icml-2025-large-language-models-to-diffu.tldr: A diffusion fine-tuning method lets pretrained language models improve accuracy with additional inference steps while preserving their original weights and single-step capabilities.

paragraphs: Generating a molecule from a natural-language description requires connecting rich textual conditions to a discrete molecular structure. The paper identifies this mismatch as a challenge for conditional diffusion models. LDMol addresses it by performing generation in a latent feature space designed to retain information about molecular structure.

The central design choice is how that space is learned. A contrastive learning strategy extracts features from text data that embed distinctive structural characteristics of molecules. This gives the diffusion model a representation suited to the relationship between language and molecular structure, making the choice of latent domain a core part of the generation method.

On a text-to-molecule benchmark, LDMol outperforms existing autoregressive baselines. The authors present this as evidence that a better latent representation can enable diffusion to surpass autoregressive approaches in this textual generation setting. They also demonstrate molecule-to-text retrieval and text-guided molecule editing. These additional applications show that the learned representation supports connections between descriptions and molecules beyond generating a new molecule from an initial prompt.
icml-2025-ldmol-a-text-to-molecule-diffu.tldr: LDMol uses a structurally informative latent space to improve text-conditioned molecular diffusion and outperform autoregressive baselines on the evaluated benchmark.

paragraphs: Robustness verification commonly starts with a specified input region and checks the worst output within it. LEVIS tackles the complementary problem of identifying regions containing no adversarial examples. This is difficult because the relevant input space can be high-dimensional, discontinuous, and non-convex, making its safe geometry hard to determine.

LEVIS-alpha finds one large verifiable ball that touches at least two boundaries of a bounded region. LEVIS-beta combines multiple verifiable balls to systematically capture the full verifiable space. The framework uses mixed-integer programming to compute nearest and directional adversarial points, linking the search for problematic inputs to the construction of verified regions.

For scalability, the authors combine complementary constrained optimization with a reduced mixed-integer formulation. This principled approximation achieves runtime reductions of up to seventeenfold. They also analyze properties of the balls produced by LEVIS-alpha and evaluate the framework on electrical power flow regression and image classification. The work therefore combines geometric characterization, optimization, and an explicitly approximate acceleration strategy for identifying reliable input regions.
icml-2025-levis-large-exact-verifiable-i.tldr: LEVIS constructs verifiable input regions from adversarial-free balls and offers a principled approximation that reduces verification runtime.

paragraphs: Large visual inputs can make cross-attention expensive in multimodal language models. Processing many visual tokens raises memory requirements and can require multiple GPUs. Existing distributed attention methods then incur substantial communication costs, making the transfer of data between devices a bottleneck during both training and inference.

LV-XAttn exploits an imbalance in the attention inputs: the query block is typically much smaller than the key-value blocks in these applications. It keeps the large key-value blocks on their local GPUs and moves the smaller queries between devices. This changes the communication pattern while preserving exact cross-attention. An activation recomputation technique further supports longer visual contexts.

The authors analyze the communication advantages and show that speedups are possible across a wide range of models. Evaluations with Llama 3-V, mPLUG-Owl3, and OpenFlamingo achieve up to 10.62 times end-to-end speedup over existing approaches. The result highlights how matching distributed computation to the relative sizes of attention inputs can improve overall performance, with the reported maximum depending on the evaluated configuration.
icml-2025-lv-xattn-distributed-cross-att.tldr: LV-XAttn accelerates exact distributed cross-attention by exchanging small query blocks while keeping large visual key-value blocks local.

paragraphs: Many mathematical datasets cover educational problems, but fewer reflect the open-ended work of professional mathematicians. This paper introduces the Algebraic Combinatorics Dataset Repository to address that gap. Its focus is conjecturing: using examples to propose mathematical relationships worth investigating, at a level associated with foundational results and open research problems.

The repository contains nine datasets in algebraic combinatorics, which studies discrete structures connected to abstract algebra. Each combines an open-ended research question with a large collection of examples, reaching ten million examples in some cases. This arrangement places the task of discovering a plausible relationship at the center of the dataset.

The authors describe several ways machine learning could engage with these resources. One route trains specialized models and analyzes them for interpretable patterns; another uses language models for program synthesis. The paper also discusses challenges in constructing such datasets. Its contribution is a collection and accompanying research framework for studying conjecture generation, rather than a reported claim that models have resolved the included open problems.
icml-2025-machine-learning-meets-algebra.tldr: The ACD Repo provides nine research-level datasets for generating mathematical conjectures from large collections of algebraic-combinatorial examples.

paragraphs: Matrix completion reconstructs missing entries from the entries that are observed. Additional information about the matrix can improve reconstruction, but many methods assume this side information is perfect. The paper addresses the more practical situation in which useful side information is available but does not completely describe the relevant structure.

The proposed orthogonal complement matrix completion model, OCMC, uses a projection derived from the available side information. This extends the traditional perfect-information formulation to incomplete information. The approach therefore gives partial knowledge a mathematical role in reconstruction without requiring it to satisfy the stronger completeness assumption used by earlier models.

Using probably approximately correct learning theory, the authors derive a sample-complexity result that decreases quadratically with the completeness level. This links the amount of side information to the number of observations needed for learning. They also develop a linearized Lagrangian solver with convergence guarantees. Experiments on synthetic data and real applications report better performance than state-of-the-art methods, supporting the value of explicitly modeling incomplete side information.
icml-2025-matrix-completion-with-incompl.tldr: OCMC reconstructs missing matrix entries using incomplete side information, with sample-complexity analysis and a solver backed by convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: A model that appears fair on ordinary inputs can develop large disparities between groups after imperceptible feature changes. This paper studies adversarial perturbations aimed at fairness alongside those aimed at accuracy. It asks how the two attack objectives relate and whether robustness against one can help protect the other.

The authors propose a unified structure for attacks covering common group-fairness notions. Within their theoretical treatment, they prove equivalences between attacks against different fairness notions and derive connections to attacks against accuracy. This provides a shared basis for analyzing vulnerabilities that might otherwise be treated as separate problems.

From the defense perspective, the paper establishes an alignment in which robustness against attacks on one objective enhances robustness against attacks on the other. That result motivates an adversarial training method addressing both objectives, and experiments report improved robustness for both. The claim concerns fairness and accuracy under adversarial perturbation; its significance is that the analyzed defenses can reinforce each other, giving a basis for joint robust training.
icml-2025-on-the-alignment-between-fairn.tldr: The paper connects adversarial attacks on fairness and accuracy and develops joint training that improves robustness to both.

paragraphs: Applying formal inference rules to natural-language statements can produce conclusions that people would not normally accept given common sense or factual knowledge. The paper calls these cases rulebreakers. It introduces RULEBREAKERS, a dataset designed to test whether language models distinguish them from ordinary cases and respond in a knowledge-informed, human-like way.

The authors evaluate seven language models and find that most achieve mediocre accuracy. The models also show some tendency to apply logical rules too rigidly compared with typical human reasoning. The evaluation thus probes whether a model can recognize when the surrounding knowledge changes what constitutes a reasonable conclusion.

Further analysis suggests that the failures may be associated with weak use of world knowledge and with attention distribution patterns. These are proposed associations, rather than established causes. The study also raises a concern for methods that use formal logic to strengthen general reasoning: increasing rule adherence could widen the gap from human-like judgments in these scenarios. The dataset makes that tension available for systematic evaluation.
icml-2025-rulebreakers-challenging-llms-.tldr: RULEBREAKERS tests when language models should temper formal inference with world knowledge and finds that many models apply rules too rigidly.

paragraphs: Image retrieval models can favor superficial similarities such as color over the semantic content of a scene. SCENIR approaches retrieval through scene graphs, emphasizing the content and structure represented in those graphs. It also addresses the inconsistent supervision that can arise when graph similarity is inferred from differently encoded image captions.

The method uses an unsupervised graph autoencoder, removing the need for labeled training pairs in its retrieval framework. The authors additionally advocate Graph Edit Distance as a deterministic, robust reference measure of scene-graph similarity. This changes both how the retrieval representation is learned and how semantic similarity is evaluated.

The paper reports stronger retrieval metrics and runtime efficiency than existing vision-based, multimodal, and supervised graph-neural-network approaches. It also applies automated scene-graph generation to unannotated datasets and demonstrates advances in counterfactual image retrieval. These findings support the usefulness of graph-based semantic representations beyond manually annotated collections. The contribution brings unsupervised learning and a graph-defined evaluation reference together to make retrieval less dependent on surface appearance and caption-based supervision.
icml-2025-scenir-visual-semantic-clarity.tldr: SCENIR uses unsupervised scene-graph representations for semantic image retrieval and proposes Graph Edit Distance as a more consistent evaluation reference.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether harmful model responses actually help ordinary users carry out harmful actions, alongside whether vulnerabilities appear in simple interactions. Its focus shifts evaluation toward the usefulness of an unsafe answer. The authors identify actionability and informativeness as two attributes that make such responses more enabling.

They introduce HarmScore to measure how effectively a response facilitates harmful actions. They also propose Speak Easy, a framework based on multi-step, multilingual interaction. The abstract reports that these interaction patterns can elicit the two response attributes, connecting a behavioral vulnerability with a metric intended to capture its practical significance.

When added to direct-request and jailbreak baselines, Speak Easy produces average absolute increases of 0.319 in attack success rate and 0.426 in HarmScore across four safety benchmarks. The evaluations include open-source and proprietary models. These findings indicate that common interaction patterns can expose substantial safety weaknesses in the tested systems. They also show why evaluating whether a response is harmful and how enabling it is can provide complementary information.
icml-2025-speak-easy-eliciting-harmful-j.tldr: Speak Easy exposes safety weaknesses in simple multilingual interactions, while HarmScore measures how effectively harmful responses enable action.

paragraphs: Generating synthetic tabular data requires reproducing relationships among columns as well as the behavior of individual columns. Deep generative approaches can do this, but they often demand substantial computation and careful parameter tuning. TabSDS explores a lightweight alternative based on direct transformations of the data rather than a trained generative model.

The method is fully non-parametric and model free. It uses rank transformations and data shuffling to produce synthetic records whose joint probability distribution closely approximates that of the original data. The joint-distribution objective matters because it concerns how variables occur together, which is central to retaining the structure of a table.

The authors compare TabSDS with multiple baselines from the Synthcity library across several datasets. They report very competitive performance, including against TabDDPM, alongside execution times orders of magnitude lower than deep generative baselines. It is also considerably faster than adversarial random forests. These results suggest that the evaluated data-generation tasks can benefit from a simple transformation-based approach with substantially lower computational demands.
icml-2025-tabsds-a-lightweight-fully-non.tldr: TabSDS generates competitive synthetic tabular data through rank and shuffling transformations, with much shorter execution times than evaluated generative baselines.

paragraphs: A reconstructed 3D object can convey different semantic information from different viewpoints. The paper argues that directly projecting two-dimensional semantic features onto 3D Gaussians overlooks this variation. A representation built that way may fail to bring together the different meanings visible across views of the same object.

LaGa addresses this by decomposing the scene into objects and establishing semantic connections across their views. It then clusters semantic descriptors and adjusts their weights using information from multiple viewpoints. These steps produce aggregated representations that draw on the differing semantic evidence available across images, making the object the point of connection between views.

Experiments show that LaGa captures useful information from viewpoint-dependent semantics and supports more comprehensive scene understanding. On LERF-OVS, the authors report a +18.7% mIoU improvement over the previous state of the art under the same settings. The result supports the value of explicitly organizing and combining cross-view semantic information when extending Gaussian-splatting reconstructions to language-driven, open-vocabulary understanding of 3D scenes.
icml-2025-tackling-view-dependent-semant.tldr: LaGa improves language-based 3D scene understanding by connecting and aggregating the different semantics an object presents across viewpoints.

paragraphs: Specializing a foundation model usually requires task data and another round of fine-tuning, with associated training costs and sensitivity to settings. Text-to-LoRA changes the adaptation step: a user describes the desired task in natural language, and a trained model generates a LoRA adapter for that task.

T2L is a hypernetwork, meaning its output supplies parameters for another model's adaptation. It constructs an adapter in one inexpensive forward pass. The authors train it using a suite of nine pretrained LoRA adapters, including ones for GSM8K and Arc. The quick adaptation therefore comes after learning how to generate adapters from existing task-specific examples.

On the corresponding test sets, the generated adapters match the performance of task-specific adapters. The authors also report that T2L can compress hundreds of adapter instances and generalize without task-specific examples to entirely unseen tasks. These findings support natural language as an interface for inexpensive specialization. The main shift is that producing an adapter becomes a prediction performed by a previously trained hypernetwork.
icml-2025-text-to-lora-instant-transform.tldr: Text-to-LoRA generates task-specific adapters from natural-language descriptions in a single forward pass, with demonstrated transfer to unseen tasks.

paragraphs: Transferring reinforcement learning across tasks requires accounting for both what the tasks share and how they differ. This paper models transition dynamics as the sum of a low-rank shared component and a sparse task-specific component. That composite structure relaxes the assumption that the full dynamics must be purely low-rank.

The proposed UCB-TQL algorithm targets tasks with shared core linear dynamics and differences confined to sparse dimensions. After learning from sufficient source-task trajectories, it applies that shared structure to a target task while adapting to the sparse differences. The source-data requirement and the assumed form of task relatedness are central to the guarantee.

The authors derive a target-task regret bound of order sqrt(e H^5 N), up to logarithmic factors, where N counts target trajectories and e measures sparse differences. The bound is independent of the ambient dimension. Within the proposed framework, this yields a substantial improvement over single-task learning. The theoretical result makes the benefit of transfer depend on structured task differences, giving a precise account of when shared dynamics can reduce learning difficulty.
icml-2025-transfer-q-learning-with-compo.tldr: UCB-TQL provides dimension-independent transfer regret guarantees when tasks share low-rank dynamics, differ sparsely, and sufficient source data are available.

paragraphs: Extending a text-to-image diffusion model to several image tasks can require expensive retraining or additional parameters. That growth makes deployment on devices more difficult. Multi-Task Upcycling addresses the problem by restructuring parts of a pretrained model so that it can support multiple image-to-image generation tasks without the same parameter inflation.

MTU replaces feed-forward layers with smaller feed-forward networks called experts and combines them with dynamic routing. This organization provides multiple expert components within the model while controlling the size of the replacement layers. The architectural change connects multi-task support directly to the computational constraints motivating the work.

Across image editing, super-resolution, and inpainting, the authors report performance comparable to separately fine-tuned single-task diffusion models. Latency and computational load, measured in GFLOPs, also remain similar to those single-task models. These findings support the possibility of consolidating several capabilities without a corresponding increase in per-use computation. The contribution is a recipe that combines multi-task diffusion with the parameter and runtime considerations relevant to on-device use.
icml-2025-upcycling-text-to-image-diffus.tldr: Multi-Task Upcycling uses smaller routed experts to add image-generation tasks while maintaining performance and computational costs comparable to single-task models.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a variational learning objective with one adjustable parameter for estimating approximate fractional posteriors. The objective remains a lower bound on the data evidence, connecting posterior approximation to a quantity used to assess probabilistic models. The authors extend the construction to hierarchical settings and ordinary Bayes posteriors.

They identify two cases where gradients can be calculated analytically. In simulations with mixture models, the fractional posteriors can achieve better calibration than posteriors obtained with the conventional variational bound. This finding concerns the quality of uncertainty estimates, adding a reason to consider the alternative objective beyond its mathematical formulation.

Applied to variational autoencoders, the method obtains higher evidence bounds and jointly learns high-performing approximate Bayes and fractional posteriors. The authors also find that training with fractional posteriors produces decoders better aligned with generation from the prior. Together, these results connect the choice of posterior-learning objective with uncertainty calibration, evidence bounds, and the behavior of a generative model when it produces samples from its prior.
icml-2025-variational-learning-of-fracti.tldr: A new variational objective learns fractional posteriors, with reported benefits for calibration, evidence bounds, and prior-based generation in VAEs.

paragraphs: Video generators can produce convincing appearances while struggling with coherent movement. The paper attributes this imbalance to conventional pixel reconstruction training, which favors appearance fidelity over motion coherence. VideoJAM addresses that training signal by encouraging a single learned representation to capture both what a scene looks like and how it moves.

During training, the model predicts generated pixels and their corresponding motion from the shared representation. During inference, Inner-Guidance uses the model's own evolving motion prediction to steer generation toward coherent movement. These two parts connect motion learning with motion-aware generation, giving the model a guidance signal that changes as the video is produced.

The authors state that VideoJAM can be applied to any video model with minimal adaptations, without changing training data or increasing model scale. They report state-of-the-art motion coherence, including improvements over competitive proprietary models, alongside better perceived visual quality. The findings support treating appearance and motion as complementary learning targets: in the evaluated systems, strengthening motion representation also improves how the generated videos look.
icml-2025-videojam-joint-appearance-moti.tldr: VideoJAM jointly learns appearance and motion, then uses its own motion predictions to improve coherence and perceived video quality.
